fuente.titulo: Cajamarca está de fiesta con su carnaval

nota: De las que se escuchan en toda la ciudad apenas empieza febrero.

en.glosa: Lima, city of kings; Trujillo, city of eternal spring; and my lovely Cajamarca, capital of carnival.
en.nota: One of the coplas heard all over the city as soon as February begins.

versos: para el grande, para el chico,
para el pobre, para el rico.

fuente.titulo: Las alegres y pícaras coplas de Cajamarca

nota: También se canta al revés: «carnaval es para el chico y el grande, para el rico y el pobre».

en.glosa: God made carnival for everyone—for the tall and the small, for the poor and the rich.
en.nota: Also sung in reverse order: “carnival is for the small and the tall, for the rich and the poor.”

nota: Se canta repitiendo cada par de versos.

en.glosa: Fate that brought me here from my homeland—just as you brought me, take me back again.
en.nota: Sung by repeating each pair of lines together.

versos: yo te sigo por tu tras.
nota: Suena cuando la fiesta se acaba, cada verso con su repetición.

en.glosa: Don’t leave, carnival, stay one more day; if you leave out of stubbornness, I’ll chase right after you.
en.nota: Sung as the festival wraps up, with each line repeated.

versos: el que no canta esta copla,
que se moje y que se calle.

en.glosa: Tune up your guitar, the troupe is heading out; whoever won’t sing this copla can get soaked and keep quiet.
I come from San Sebastián singing with my troupe, asking that dark-haired woman to stop drenching me.

versos: con su panza y su sombrero,
lo que juntó el año entero.

en.glosa: Ño Carnavalón has arrived with his belly and his hat, ready to spend in four days what he saved all year.

versos: que el carnaval se nos va
y la vida es cosa corta.

en.glosa: Splash me with paint, sweetheart, splash me with water—it doesn’t matter, carnival slips away and life is short.

nota: En Cajamarca el «poto» es el mate de calabaza en que se sirve la chicha. El doble sentido es marca de la casa.

en.glosa: Give me chicha from your poto, don’t give me that look—I’m talking about a gourd, and your mind is racing.
en.nota: In Cajamarca, a poto is the dried gourd bowl used to serve chicha (and slang for backside in Peru). Double entendres are a carnival staple.

versos: que mi barrio con su copla
te deja muda en una hora.

en.glosa: Troupe from the other neighborhood, don’t act like such big singers—my neighborhood’s coplas will leave you speechless in an hour.

versos: que hasta el misho de mi casa
nota: «Misho» es gato en el habla de Cajamarca.

en.glosa: Hush, hush, little singer, stop bragging so much—even the cat (misho) at my house meows your tune better.
Girl from Cumbemayo, your eyes are two bright stars; if you glance my way, I’ll give you all my sheep.

versos: no me eches más agua fría,
nota: «Chinasha» y «cholasho»: muchachita y muchachito, con el diminutivo -ash- que viene del culle.

en.glosa: Dark-eyed girl (chinashita), don’t throw any more cold water on me—this poor guy (cholashito) has no clean clothes left.
en.nota: Chinasha and cholasho mean “young girl” and “young boy,” using the -ash- diminutive inherited from the extinct Culle language.

en.glosa: Right here (aquisito) it rains, right here the sun comes out, right here you got drenched—and right here, what color!
Cajamarca, lovely land of fresh curd cheese and manjar blanco—anyone who tastes you at carnival can never forget you.

nota: La «shulca» es la hija menor, la última de la familia.

en.glosa: The youngest girl (shulquita) in my house stole my paint—the smallest kid in the neighborhood with the biggest mischief.
en.nota: Shulca means the youngest child in a family.

en.glosa: Ño Carnavalón is leaving, all his “widows” are weeping—and in his will he leaves us nothing but debts and a thousand doubts.

versos: ya te vas y aquí me quedo,
con la pintura en la cara
y en el bolsillo, ni un medio.

en.glosa: Goodbye, goodbye, carnival—you’re leaving and here I stay, with paint still on my face and not a coin left in my pocket.
